modeling_assumptions.text: Each tablet (iPad) line is priced at the carrier's flat listed additional-tablet-line rate (Appendix C), applied per tablet -- for Verizon this is now the tier-matched Unlimited Plus tablet rate ($25.00/mo, the tier matching the family's recommended Unlimited Plus smartphone plan), for AT&T the flat $20.00/mo rate. Re-verified 2026-08-18: the live Verizon page does document a real first-vs-additional-tablet asymmetry that this flat-rate model does NOT capture -- only one connected-device line per account gets Verizon's 50% existing-smartphone discount on a non-Ultimate plan like Unlimited Plus, so a real Markenan bill would show one tablet at $25.00/mo and the second at the full $50.00/mo ($75.00/mo total, not $50.00/mo flat). This case knowingly keeps the simpler flat-rate model (both tablets at $25.00/mo) for consistency with AT&T's own flat, unlimited-quantity $20.00/mo rate and because a per-tablet 'which one gets the discount' rule adds complexity beyond this case's grade band without changing which carrier wins -- disclosed here rather than silently modeled away.

Oregon's Tax Foundation-published combined wireless tax/fee rate (Appendix D) is applied as a single multiplier to the full pre-tax monthly bill (phone lines plus tablet lines together), rather than modeling which specific charges are percentage-based versus flat per-line fees separately -- real bills mix both, but the published figure is already a single blended rate, matching the precision this case's public data actually supports.

balance.argument_a: Verizon Plus is the carrier extended family already recommended, and its 30GB of mobile hotspot data is a real, usable amount for a salesperson checking email and pulling up account records between clinic visits. Verizon also has the larger nationwide 4G LTE network by a real, sourced margin -- about 70% of U.S. land area covered versus AT&T's 68% (Appendix E/S8) -- and that rural-coverage edge is concentrated in exactly the kind of stretches (Burns, Astoria, Florence) Jake is about to start driving through four days a week, where AT&T Extra 2.0's cheaper price and larger hotspot allowance do the family no good if the signal itself is not there.
balance.argument_b: AT&T Extra 2.0 is cheaper than Verizon Plus at every phone-line count the family will actually reach -- 2, 3, and 4 lines -- both before and after tablets and Oregon's wireless tax are added in. It also includes substantially more mobile hotspot data (50GB vs. 30GB), which speaks directly to Jake's stated need to hotspot a laptop from the road multiple days a week.
balance.margin_basis: Total monthly family bill (2 phone lines + 2 tablet lines, Oregon's 22.53% combined wireless tax/fee rate applied) for Verizon Unlimited Plus vs. AT&T Unlimited Extra 2.0 -- both plans real, sourced, current, and the only plans on either carrier that actually include mobile hotspot data, the family's stated hard requirement (Appendices A-D). See derived{} for the full worked figures.

context_glossary.desc: A mobile hotspot lets a phone share its own cellular data connection with other devices (like a laptop), turning the phone into a mini Wi-Fi router. This is exactly what Jake needs to get his laptop online from hotel rooms and rental cars instead of home internet.

AutoPay is a carrier program where a customer authorizes automatic monthly bill payment (usually from a bank account), in exchange for a per-line discount off the plan's listed price. Both carriers' Appendix A/B prices in this case already assume AutoPay and paperless billing are enrolled.

The Universal Service Fund is a federal fee, collected from telecom companies and passed on to customers, that helps pay for affordable phone and broadband access in rural and low-income areas nationwide. It is the largest single piece of the federal portion of Appendix D's Oregon wireless tax/fee rate.

Roaming is what happens when a phone connects to a different carrier's network because it is outside its home carrier's coverage area, such as when Jake drives into Canada. Roaming can normally cost extra, which is why Appendix E specifically notes that Canada/Mexico roaming is included at no additional charge on both carriers' eligible plans.
